title: How modern language models work
description: From text to tokens, attention, sampling, retrieval and tools: how a large language model turns a prompt into an answer, and what it does not do along the way.

parts.title: Learning, and what the words mean

nodes.title: Text
nodes.summary: A language model never reads letters directly: before it can do anything, text has to become a sequence of integers.
searchTerms: how does an llm read text
learningObjectives: Explain why a neural network cannot consume text as written
Name the steps between a string and the model's first computation
misconceptions: A language model reads the letters of a prompt the way a person does.

nodes.title: Tokenization
nodes.summary: Text is split into units from a fixed vocabulary: whole words, pieces of words, or raw bytes.
learningObjectives: Describe how a subword tokenizer splits common and rare words
Explain why token counts differ between models
misconceptions: One token is one word.

nodes.title: Token IDs
nodes.summary: Each token is replaced by its position in the vocabulary. The number is an index, and carries no meaning of its own.
learningObjectives: Explain why token IDs are indices rather than quantities
misconceptions: Tokens with nearby IDs have similar meanings.

nodes.title: Embeddings
nodes.summary: Token IDs select rows of a learned table of vectors: the model's starting point for each token, not its final word on meaning.
learningObjectives: Describe what an embedding table is and how it is used
Distinguish a token's input embedding from its contextual representation
misconceptions: An embedding is a fixed definition of what a word means.

nodes.title: Positional information
nodes.summary: Attention on its own ignores word order, so position has to be injected. Most current models do it by rotating queries and keys (RoPE).
learningObjectives: Explain why a transformer needs positional information
Contrast absolute position embeddings with rotary embeddings
misconceptions: Every model adds a position vector to each token embedding.

nodes.title: Context-dependent representations
nodes.summary: As vectors pass through the network, each token's representation is rewritten using the tokens around it.
learningObjectives: Explain how the same token ends up with different vectors in different sentences
Describe where contextual representations exist and how long they last
misconceptions: The meaning of a word in context is looked up from a stored table.

nodes.title: Transformer layers
nodes.summary: A transformer is a stack of blocks. Each one lets tokens exchange information (attention), then transforms every token on its own (an MLP).
learningObjectives: Name the two sublayers of a transformer block and what each does
Explain why the same weights can process inputs of any length
misconceptions: Each layer of the model handles a different word of the input.

nodes.title: Self-attention
nodes.summary: Each token's representation gathers information from other positions in the context, weighted by how relevant the model computes them to be.
learningObjectives: Explain what attention computes for one position
State the scope of what attention can reach
misconceptions: Attention lets the model look things up beyond what is in its context.

nodes.title: Queries, keys and values
nodes.summary: Each token is projected into a query (what it looks for), a key (what it can be matched on) and a value (what it passes along).
learningObjectives: Write down scaled dot-product attention and explain each term
Explain why keys and values are what gets cached
misconceptions: Attention selects one matching token, like a database lookup.

nodes.title: Dense attention
nodes.summary: In full (dense) attention every token can attend to every earlier token, so the work grows with the square of the sequence length.
learningObjectives: Explain why attention cost grows quadratically with length
Distinguish exact optimisations like FlashAttention from approximations
misconceptions: FlashAttention is an approximation of attention.

nodes.title: Sparse and sliding-window attention
nodes.summary: Some attention layers restrict each token to a window or pattern of positions, trading direct reach for lower cost. It all happens inside the model.
learningObjectives: Describe sliding-window attention and how information still travels beyond the window
Explain why sparse attention is not a form of retrieval
misconceptions: Sparse attention fetches the relevant parts of a long document, like search.

nodes.title: Context windows
nodes.summary: The context window is the most tokens a model can process at once: prompt, documents, tool results and its own output together.
learningObjectives: Define the context window precisely
Explain why a larger context window does not remove the need for retrieval
misconceptions: The context window is a slice of the model's embeddings.
Everything inside the context window is used equally well.
A large enough context window makes retrieval unnecessary.

nodes.title: KV cache
nodes.summary: During generation, keys and values already computed for earlier tokens are kept and reused, so each new token only computes its own.
learningObjectives: Explain what the KV cache stores and why it speeds up generation
Estimate how KV cache memory grows with context length
State what the KV cache does not contain
misconceptions: The KV cache stores alternative completions the model considered.
The KV cache is a form of long-term memory or learning.

seeAlso.title: What happens to the tokens not chosen

nodes.title: Logits
nodes.summary: The final representation at the last position is turned into one score per vocabulary entry: the logits.
learningObjectives: Describe how a hidden state becomes a score for every token in the vocabulary
misconceptions: Logits are probabilities.

nodes.title: Probabilities and softmax
nodes.summary: Softmax turns the logits into a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary.
learningObjectives: Compute softmax for a small list of logits
Explain why a high probability is not the same as a correct answer
misconceptions: A token with high probability is likely to be factually correct.

nodes.title: Decoding and sampling
nodes.summary: Generation is a loop: choose one token from the distribution, append it to the input, run the model again.
searchTerms: how does an llm generate text
learningObjectives: Describe the autoregressive generation loop
Explain why decoding settings belong to the inference software rather than the model
misconceptions: The model writes a whole answer at once and then displays it word by word.

seeAlso.title: What happens to the tokens not chosen

nodes.title: Temperature, top-k and top-p
nodes.summary: Temperature reshapes the distribution; top-k and top-p cut off its unlikely tail before a token is drawn.
learningObjectives: Describe the effect of temperature, top-k and top-p on the next-token distribution
misconceptions: Raising the temperature makes the model think more creatively.

nodes.title: What happens to the tokens not chosen
nodes.summary: Next-token candidates that were not chosen are normally discarded. The model does not keep them as alternative lines of reasoning.
learningObjectives: Explain why ordinary decoding produces exactly one sequence
Distinguish implicit alternatives in a distribution from explicitly generated alternatives
misconceptions: During generation the model explores several answers in parallel and keeps the best one.

nodes.title: Multiple samples, search and verification
nodes.summary: Systems can explore alternatives deliberately: generate several candidates, search over partial solutions, and check the results. It is an outer loop around generation.
learningObjectives: Describe best-of-n sampling and self-consistency
Explain why multi-candidate search is an outer loop rather than part of token generation
misconceptions: Running more candidates at inference time trains the model.

buildsOn.title: What happens to the tokens not chosen

nodes.title: Quantization
nodes.summary: Quantization stores a model's weights in fewer bits, such as 8 or 4 instead of 16, trading a little accuracy for a model that is smaller and faster to read.
learningObjectives: Estimate the memory a model's weights need at a given precision
Explain what per-block scales do and why quality usually survives 8 and 4 bits
misconceptions: A quantized model is a smaller model trained separately from the original.

nodes.title: Running a model on your own hardware
nodes.summary: Whether a model runs locally is mostly a question of memory: it must hold the weights and the KV cache, and generation speed is set by how fast those weights can be read.
searchTerms: how much ram do i need
why is my local model slow
learningObjectives: Estimate whether a model fits in a machine's memory
Explain why generation speed follows memory bandwidth rather than processor speed
misconceptions: Faster processor cores are what make a local model generate faster.

nodes.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
nodes.summary: RAG searches an external collection at request time and places the most relevant passages in the context before the model answers.
learningObjectives: Walk through the steps of a RAG pipeline
Name the main ways a RAG system fails
misconceptions: RAG teaches the model new facts by updating it.

nodes.title: Retrieval versus attention
nodes.summary: Attention mixes information among tokens already in the context. Retrieval decides which outside information gets into the context at all.
searchTerms: does a bigger context window replace rag
learningObjectives: Contrast attention and retrieval by where they run and what they operate on
Explain why sparse attention and long contexts do not replace retrieval
misconceptions: Attention and retrieval are the same thing at different scales.
A long enough context window makes retrieval unnecessary.

nodes.title: External memory
nodes.summary: Anything a system should remember beyond one context window has to be stored outside the model and read back in as tokens.
learningObjectives: Explain why a model has no memory across requests by itself
Describe how memory features are built from storage and retrieval
misconceptions: A chat assistant remembers you because the model learned from your earlier conversations.

nodes.title: Tool use
nodes.summary: A model can emit a structured request to call a tool. Software outside the model runs it and feeds the result back into the context.
learningObjectives: Describe the loop between a model and the application that runs its tool calls
Explain where tool execution and permissions actually live
misconceptions: The model itself executes the code or API calls it requests.

nodes.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
nodes.summary: MCP is an open protocol for exposing tools, data and prompts to AI applications. It standardises the connection, not the retrieval.
learningObjectives: Describe the parts of an MCP connection and what a server can expose
Explain why MCP is not itself retrieval or memory
misconceptions: MCP is a kind of RAG.
MCP gives the model direct access to systems.

nodes.title: Codebase-aware retrieval
nodes.summary: Coding agents find the relevant parts of a repository with search tools, such as text search, symbol indexes, embeddings or code graphs, and read them into context.
searchTerms: how do coding agents understand a codebase
learningObjectives: List the main ways an agent searches a codebase and when each works best
Explain why exact identifiers favour lexical search
misconceptions: A coding agent reads and understands the whole repository at once.

nodes.title: Inference versus training
nodes.summary: Training changes a model's weights. Inference, meaning ordinary use, runs fixed weights and changes nothing in the model.
searchTerms: does chatgpt learn from my conversations
does the model learn while chatting
learningObjectives: Distinguish what changes during training from what changes during inference
Explain in-context learning without weight updates
misconceptions: A model learns from each conversation as it happens.
In-context learning updates the model's weights.

nodes.title: Hallucination
nodes.summary: A model can state something false as fluently as something true, because it generates likely text and has no store of facts to check against.
searchTerms: why does ai make things up
learningObjectives: Explain why fluent output is no evidence that it is correct
Name the main ways systems reduce hallucination, and what each depends on
misconceptions: A model looks facts up in an internal database, and a hallucination is the wrong row coming back.
When a model hallucinates, it knows the answer is false and says it anyway.

nodes.title: Self-training and synthetic data
nodes.summary: Model outputs that have been filtered, checked or ranked can become training data for a later model: a learning loop outside generation.
learningObjectives: Describe a generate, verify and train loop
Explain why verification quality limits self-training
misconceptions: A model improves itself every time it generates and checks an answer.

nodes.title: Recursive self-improvement
nodes.summary: The idea that an AI system could improve its own capabilities, including its ability to improve itself. A research concept, not a current mechanism.
learningObjectives: State the recursive self-improvement hypothesis
Identify which parts of today's training loops resemble it, and which do not
misconceptions: Current models rewrite their own weights to become smarter while they run.

nodes.title: AGI, and why definitions vary
nodes.summary: Artificial general intelligence has no single agreed definition, so any claim about it depends on which definition is being used.
learningObjectives: Compare several definitions of AGI
Evaluate an AGI claim by identifying the definition and the measurement behind it
misconceptions: AGI is a well-defined threshold that a model either passes or does not.
